label: Prediksjon 1
note: Den mest sannsynlige eksamenen etter prediksjonen: to teorioppgaver og fire regneoppgaver med kapitalstruktur, verdsetting, realopsjon og oppkjøp. Ta den på tid med penn og papir.
facts: Prediction exam in Kurbatov's format: 6 exercises, 100 points, 180 minutes, no multiple choice, calculator and one bilingual dictionary permitted.
Points per exercise: 10 · 10 · 20 · 20 · 20 · 20. Two verbal exercises with sentence budgets, then four computational exercises.
The formula sheet is handed out.
Recommended precision: 4 decimal places. An error carried forward is not penalised again in later parts.
Written for this app from the prediction of the 2026 exam. Every number in the solutions is computed in a script.

exercises.title: Governance
exercises.merke: Som H2025 E2, i formen fra forelesning 17 · governance som teori 90 %
exercises.body:
You manage Gudenå Pension, a Danish pension fund that has just become the largest shareholder, with 9% of the votes, in Kallmar Robotics Inc., a widely held company listed in New York. Its board has just hired a new CEO from outside.

As the largest owner, you want the new CEO to act in the shareholders' interest without scaring the CEO into avoiding every risk. Select three measures you would push for and explain each in 2–3 sentences: how it works and why it fits Kallmar (3 points each). Then add one sentence on how one of your measures could backfire if pushed too far (1 point).
exercises.solution:
1. Pay the new CEO in long-term shares. A large part of the pay comes as restricted shares that vest over four to five years, with a clawback if results are later restated. The new CEO arrives with no stake in Kallmar, so this makes the CEO gain and lose with the long-run share price, just like the fund. Shares reward sensible long-term risks without paying for pure gambles as many options would; a solid fixed salary means one bad year does not ruin the CEO, so the CEO is not scared away from all risk.

2. Make the board independent. With 9% of the votes the fund can nominate one or two independent directors to a board of about 7 to 11 and push for a chair who is not the CEO, with independent pay, audit and nomination committees. Such a board can question the new CEO's plans, set the pay and replace the CEO without personal ties getting in the way; the lecture calls an independent board «one of the first check marks» (recording 17, 1:19:39).

3. Transparency and a reason for the other owners to vote. Kallmar reports clear targets every quarter and holds an annual investor meeting where the largest holders question the CEO, while proxy access in the bylaws lets large owners nominate directors. Thousands of small investors cannot be made to vote, but the institutions can be drawn in by meetings and direct contact (recording 17, 1:21:03 to 1:21:51), so the CEO knows that the owners are watching.

Backfire (1 point). If the fund monitors too tightly, for example by asking the board to approve every investment, the CEO will do only the safest minimum and new robotics projects will not be started (recording 17, 1:17:10).

Why the setting matters. The fund captures 9% of any value it creates, so monitoring pays for it, while the small holders free-ride. That is why the fund, not the dispersed owners, has to drive all three measures.

Also accepted. Options with their drawback (they reward risk); a bonus on targets that cannot be gamed (an EPS target met through a buyback does not count); a golden parachute if Kallmar needs the CEO to take R&D risk; limits on perks; a shareholder proposal; an activist campaign if the CEO underperforms. As in Kurbatov's H2025 key, any reasonable measure with an explanation earns the points.
criteria: Three distinct measures, 2–3 sentences each, 3 points each: 1 for the measure, 1 for how it makes the CEO act in the shareholders' interest and 1 for why it fits Kallmar (dispersed owners, a 9% holder, a new CEO from outside).

Any reasonable measure with an explanation is accepted (as in the H2025 key). Typical: long-term equity pay or clawbacks, an independent board and committees, a chair who is not the CEO, transparency and regular reporting, investor meetings, proxy access in the bylaws, a shareholder proposal.

«Make the shareholders vote» earns full points only with a concrete how (meetings for the institutions, communication, proxy access); small owners cannot be forced to vote (recording 17, 1:20:22 to 1:21:51).
Two versions of the same tool with the same argument count once.
1 point for the backfire sentence: monitoring that is too tight makes the CEO passive, options reward excessive risk, a large owner may push its own aims or similar.
Board size: an argument for about 7 to 11 directors is accepted; «a smaller board works better» alone is not.

exercises.title: Capital Structure
exercises.merke: Teorispørsmålet varslet i forelesning 3 · kapitalstruktur verbalt 25 %
exercises.body:
Modigliani and Miller show that in a perfect capital market the value of a firm does not depend on how it is financed. Real firms clearly care about their capital structure: most of them borrow, but few borrow as much as they could.

Choose three assumptions behind the MM result that fail in practice. For each, name the assumption and explain in 1–2 sentences what its failure implies for how much debt a firm should use (3 points each). Finish with one sentence that combines your three points into a conclusion about the amount of debt (1 point).
exercises.solution:
1. No taxes. Interest is deducted before corporate tax, so debt creates a tax shield (τcD for permanent debt) that the government pays for. On its own this pushes towards more debt, all the way to 100%.

2. No costs of financial distress. A firm that cannot pay its creditors loses value through legal costs and, more importantly, through indirect costs: assets sold in a fire sale at a heavy discount (land worth 10 million sold for 7 million in the lecture's example, recording 04, 8:16) and lost customers and suppliers. These expected costs rise with leverage, so they push towards less debt, most of all for firms with illiquid or intangible assets.

3. No agency costs (investment does not depend on financing). With risky debt, shareholders gain from risky projects at the creditors' expense (risk shifting, a wealth transfer) and may forgo positive-NPV projects whose gains would go to the creditors (debt overhang); creditors foresee this and charge for it. This pushes towards less debt, although some debt also disciplines managers who would otherwise waste free cash flow.

Conclusion (1 point). The best amount of debt trades the tax shield (and the discipline) against the expected costs of distress and the agency costs, so it lies between zero and 100% and is higher for stable, profitable firms with tangible assets.

Also accepted. Asymmetric information (an equity issue signals overvaluation, so firms prefer internal funds, then debt, then equity); transaction and issue costs; markets that are not efficient or investors who are not rational; personal taxes on interest. Each earns full points only if it says what it implies for the amount of debt.
criteria: Three distinct assumptions, 3 points each: 1 for naming the assumption and 2 for what its failure implies for the amount of debt, with the mechanism. A name alone («taxes») earns at most 1.

Taxes: the interest tax shield favours debt. Distress: direct and indirect costs (fire sales, lost customers and suppliers) rise with leverage and favour less debt. Agency: risk shifting and debt overhang favour less debt; the discipline that debt puts on free cash flow is a benefit.

Also accepted with a consequence for debt: asymmetric information (pecking order), transaction or issue costs, inefficient markets or irrational investors, personal taxes. When the question was asked in class, transaction costs, search costs and insider knowledge were all accepted (recording 03, 10:04 to 11:45).
Direct and indirect costs of distress count as one assumption; risk shifting and debt overhang count as one (agency costs).

1 point for the conclusion: an optimum between no debt and all debt, where the benefits are traded against the costs. The name «trade-off theory» is not required. «Debt is good» or «debt is bad» alone earns nothing.
«Uncertainty» alone is not a failed assumption: uncertainty exists in the MM world too (recording 03, 11:15).

exercises.title: Recapitalisation
exercises.merke: Som H2024 E3 og H2025 E3, med en vri til slutt · MM-rekapitalisering 70 %
exercises.body: Sørvær Logistikk ASA has 40 million shares outstanding at NOK 85 per share and NOK 1,100 million of debt. The debt is risk-free with an expected return equal to the risk-free rate of 3.5%. The equity cost of capital is 9.2%. Unless stated otherwise, the firm operates in a perfect capital market with no taxes (the MM propositions hold).

parts.label: a
parts.body: What is the unlevered cost of capital (rU) of the firm?
parts.solution:
Step 1. Market values. E = 40 × 85 = NOK 3,400 million, so V = E + D = 3,400 + 1,100 = NOK 4,500 million.

Step 2. Weight the two returns. With no taxes rU is the pre-tax WACC:
rU = (E/V)rE + (D/V)rD = (3,400/4,500) × 9.2% + (1,100/4,500) × 3.5%
= 0.069511 + 0.008556 = 0.078067 (7.8067%)
criteria: Market values: E = 40 × 85 = 3,400 and V = 4,500.
Weights E/V and D/V from market values, r_D = r_f = 3.5% because the debt is risk-free.
Show the calculation.

parts.label: b
parts.body:
The board announces that the firm will borrow more and use all the new debt, which is also risk-free, to repurchase shares so that its debt-to-equity ratio becomes 0.8.

How much new debt will the firm issue? What happens to the share price at the announcement? How many shares will be repurchased?
parts.solution:
Step 1. Value and price. There are no taxes or other frictions, so MM I holds: the recapitalisation only re-slices the same cash flows. V stays at NOK 4,500 million and the share price stays at NOK 85.00 on the announcement.

Step 2. New debt. D/E = 0.8 means D/V = 0.8/1.8 = 0.4444, so the target is D = 0.4444 × 4,500 = NOK 2,000 million. The firm already has 1,100, so it issues NOK 900 million of new debt.

Step 3. Shares repurchased. At the unchanged price: 900/85 = 10.5882 million shares, leaving 40 − 10.5882 = 29.4118 million.

Check. E = 4,500 − 2,000 = 2,500 over 29.4118 million shares = NOK 85.00 ✓. The two-equation route gives the same: N × P = 900 and (40 − N) × P = 2,500, so 40P = 3,400 and P = 85.00 (recording 05, 1:09:02).
criteria: Converts D/E = 0.8 into D/V = 0.4444 (or solves D = 0.8E with D + E = 4,500): target D = 2,000, new debt 900. Using 0.8 as D/V (D = 3,600) is the trap.
Share price unchanged at NOK 85 on the announcement, with the reason: MM I, no tax shield or other value is created.
Shares repurchased = 900/85 = 10.5882 million.
New debt, not total debt: answering 2,000 ignores the 1,100 already outstanding.

parts.label: c
parts.body: What is the equity cost of capital after the recapitalisation?
parts.solution:
MM II with the new D/E of 0.8 (D = 2,000, E = 2,500) and rD = rf:

rE = rU + (D/E)(rU − rD) = 7.8067% + 0.8 × (7.8067% − 3.5000%) = 7.8067% + 3.4453% = 11.2520%

Check. (2,500/4,500) × 11.2520% + (2,000/4,500) × 3.5000% = 6.2511% + 1.5556% = 7.8067% = rU ✓. This identity holds once rE came from MM II, so it only catches arithmetic slips.
criteria: MM II with D/E = 0.8, not D/V. Using D/V = 0.4444 gives 9.72% and is the D/E-versus-D/V trap.
r_D = 3.5% because the debt stays risk-free.

parts.label: d
parts.body: The CFO notes that earnings per share will rise after the buyback. Are the shareholders who keep their shares better off than before? Are they better or worse off than those who sold? Explain briefly.
parts.solution:
Nobody is better or worse off. In a perfect market the recapitalisation only re-slices the same cash flows (MM I). The price stays at NOK 85, so a seller gets NOK 85 in cash and a holder keeps a share worth NOK 85.

Why the higher EPS does not help. EPS rises because each remaining share now carries more debt, but so does its risk: rE rises from 9.2% to 11.2520%, exactly enough to leave the price unchanged. A holder who wanted the old risk could undo the extra leverage by buying some of the firm's debt (homemade leverage).

The numbers behind it (not required). If the assets earn a constant FCF forever, FCF = rU × V = 0.078067 × 4,500 = NOK 351.30 million a year. EPS before = (351.30 − 38.50)/40 = NOK 7.8200; EPS after = (351.30 − 70.00)/29.4118 = NOK 9.5642. Price = EPS/rE: 7.82/0.092 = 85.00 and 9.5642/0.112520 = 85.00.
criteria: Holders are not better off than before: the price is unchanged at 85 (MM I).
Holders and sellers are equally well off: 85 in cash or a share worth 85.
Explains why the higher EPS does not raise the price: the equity is riskier, so r_E rises (MM II) and the higher EPS is discounted at a higher rate.
Homemade leverage or the EPS numbers are a bonus, not a requirement.

parts.label: e
parts.body:
Now assume instead that Sørvær pays 22% corporate tax and announces, as a surprise, NOK 1,200 million of new permanent debt, all used to repurchase shares. All debt stays risk-free; the price of NOK 85 already reflects the tax shield on the existing debt.

What is the present value of the tax shield on the new debt? What is the share price right after the announcement?
parts.solution:
Step 1. PV of the tax shield. The new debt is permanent and risk-free, so it saves τc × rD × D = 0.22 × 0.035 × 1,200 = NOK 9.24 million of tax every year forever. Discounted at rD: PV(TS) = 9.24/0.035 = τcD = 0.22 × 1,200 = NOK 264 million.

Step 2. Price at the announcement. The market prices the shield as soon as the plan is known, before a single share is bought back. The gain goes to the current 40 million shares: E = 3,400 + 264 = 3,664, so P = 3,664/40 = NOK 91.60, a jump of 264/40 = NOK 6.60.

Compare (b): without taxes the price did not move because nothing of value was created. Here the price jumps on the announcement, not on the buyback.
criteria: PV(TS) = τD = 0.22 × 1,200 = 264, because the debt is permanent (the yearly shield of 9.24 discounted at r_D). Reporting only the yearly shield is the trap.
Price after the announcement = (3,400 + 264)/40 = 91.60: the whole gain goes to the shares outstanding at the announcement.
States that the price jumps at the announcement, before the buyback (efficient market).
Show the calculation.

parts.label: f
parts.body: How many shares will be repurchased? Who captures the value of the tax shield? Explain briefly.
parts.solution:
Shares repurchased. The buyback happens at the new price: 1,200/91.60 = 13.1004 million shares, leaving 40 − 13.1004 = 26.8996 million.

Check. After the buyback VL = 4,500 + 264 = 4,764 and D = 1,100 + 1,200 = 2,300, so E = 2,464 and 2,464/26.8996 = NOK 91.60 ✓.

Who captures the gain. All the shareholders at the announcement, in proportion to their shares: NOK 6.60 per share, whether they sell (at 91.60) or keep a share worth 91.60. The value comes from the government, which collects less tax. Dividing by the old price (1,200/85 = 14.1176 million) is the classic error: once the plan is known, nobody sells for less than the new price (recording 03, 1:00:49 to 1:01:38).
criteria: Shares repurchased at the new price: 1,200/91.60 = 13.1004 million. Dividing by 85 is the classic error.
The existing shareholders capture the whole gain at the announcement, sellers and holders alike (NOK 6.60 per share).
Bonus, not required: the value comes from lower taxes paid to the government.

exercises.title: Valuation
exercises.merke: Som H2024 E5 og H2025 E4, men for et prosjekt · WACC og APV 80 %
exercises.body:
Norrfjäll Verkstad AB (existing free cash flow SEK 85 million a year, unaffected) is evaluating a new production line for wind-turbine gearboxes.

The line costs SEK 225 million paid today (t = 0) and needs net working capital of SEK 9 million from today. In Year 1 it has revenue of SEK 60 million, operating costs (excluding depreciation) of 62% of revenue and depreciation equal to maintenance capital expenditure, 8% of revenue. All of these grow by 2% a year forever, as does net working capital (9 × 1.02 at t = 1). The tax rate is 20.6%.

The line keeps a constant debt-to-value ratio of 40% at a cost of debt of 5%. Klarälven Precision AB, a listed firm with the same business risk, has an equity beta of 1.30, a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.5 and a cost of debt of 4.5%. The risk-free rate is 3% and the expected market return is 8%.

parts.label: a
parts.body: What is the line's free cash flow in Year 1? What is the total cash outlay at t = 0?
parts.solution:
Step 1. EBIT and taxes.
Year 1SEK million
Revenue60.000
Operating costs (62%)−37.200
Depreciation (8%)−4.800
EBIT18.000
EBIT × (1 − 0.206)14.292
+ Depreciation4.800
− Capital expenditure−4.800
− ΔNWC = 9 × 1.02 − 9−0.180
FCF114.112

FCF1 = 18.0 × 0.794 + 4.8 − 4.8 − 0.18 = SEK 14.112 million. Only the change in working capital enters, not its level: «one of the biggest fallacies would be forgetting the delta» (recording 18, 12:44).

Step 2. Outlay at t = 0. The machine and the first working capital: 225 + 9 = SEK 234 million.

Norrfjäll's existing FCF of 85 is not part of the line and plays no role (recording 18, 6:41).
criteria: FCF = EBIT(1 − τ) + Dep − CapEx − ΔNWC, with depreciation added back and the 20.6% tax on EBIT.
ΔNWC in Year 1 = 9 × 1.02 − 9 = 0.18, not the level 9.18 (which gives 5.112).
FCF_1 = 14.112 and outlay at t = 0 = 225 + 9 = 234.
Uses only the line's cash flows: the existing FCF of 85 is irrelevant.

parts.label: b
parts.body: Find the debt beta of Klarälven and the unlevered cost of capital (rU) of the line.
parts.solution:
Step 1. Debt beta from the CAPM. βD = (rD − rf)/(E[RMkt] − rf) = (4.5% − 3%)/(8% − 3%) = 0.3000.

Step 2. Unlever. D/E = 0.5 gives D/V = 0.5/1.5 = 0.3333 and E/V = 0.6667:
βU = 0.6667 × 1.30 + 0.3333 × 0.30 = 0.8667 + 0.1000 = 0.9667
rU = 3% + 0.9667 × 5% = 7.8333%

Same answer through returns. rE of Klarälven = 3% + 1.30 × 5% = 9.5%, so rU = 0.6667 × 9.5% + 0.3333 × 4.5% = 7.8333% ✓. The line has the same business risk, so it has the same rU. No tax enters rU.
criteria: β_D = (4.5% − 3%)/5% = 0.30; the market risk premium is 5%, not 8%.
D/E = 0.5 converted to D/V = 1/3 before weighting.
r_U = 7.8333% through betas or returns; no (1 − τ) in r_U.
Setting β_D = 0 although r_D > r_f understates r_U.

parts.label: c
parts.body: Find the line's equity cost of capital and its after-tax WACC (rwacc).
parts.solution:
Step 1. rE with the line's own leverage. D/V = 0.40 gives D/E = 0.40/0.60 = 0.6667; the line borrows at its own rD of 5%:
rE = 7.8333% + 0.6667 × (7.8333% − 5%) = 7.8333% + 1.8889% = 9.7222%

Step 2. After-tax WACC. rwacc = 0.60 × 9.7222% + 0.40 × 5% × (1 − 0.206) = 5.8333% + 1.5880% = 7.4213%

Quick check. rU − d·τc·rD = 7.8333% − 0.40 × 0.206 × 5% = 7.8333% − 0.4120% = 7.4213% ✓ (an identity that catches arithmetic slips).

The traps. Klarälven's D/E of 0.5 gives rE = 9.25% and rwacc = 7.49%; Klarälven's rD of 4.5% gives rwacc = 7.46%. Both describe Klarälven's financing, not the line's.
criteria: Uses the line's own D/V of 40% (D/E = 0.6667) and its own r_D of 5%, not Klarälven's 0.5 and 4.5%.
r_E = 9.7222% from MM II.
r_wacc = 7.4213%, with (1 − τ) on r_D only.
Weights 0.6 and 0.4; using D/E = 0.6667 as a weight is the trap.

parts.label: d
parts.body: What is the NPV of the line using the WACC method?
parts.solution:
Step 1. Value of the future cash flows. FCF grows at 2% forever, so VL0 = FCF1/(rwacc − g) = 14.112/(0.074213 − 0.02) = 14.112/0.054213 = SEK 260.3050 million.

Step 2. NPV. NPV = VL0 − outlay = 260.3050 − 234 = SEK 26.3050 million. The line is worth doing.

The question asks for the project's NPV: VL alone (the PV) or a value for Norrfjäll as a whole does not answer it («if it says evaluate the project, I want the NPV of the project», recording 18, 7:13).
criteria: Growing perpetuity at r_wacc − g with FCF_1 (not FCF_0).
V^L = 260.3050 and NPV = 26.3050 after subtracting the outlay of 234, including the working capital.
Reporting the PV (260.31) or adding the existing business loses the points for NPV.

parts.label: e
parts.body: What is the line's debt capacity today? Using this debt, find the NPV of the line with the APV method.
parts.solution:
Step 1. Debt capacity. Debt is 40% of the value of the line's future cash flows: D0 = 0.40 × VL0 = 0.40 × 260.3050 = SEK 104.1220 million. It is a share of the PV, not of the NPV and not of Norrfjäll as a whole. As the line's value grows at 2%, so does the debt (D1 = 106.2044).

Step 2. Unlevered value. VU = 14.112/(0.078333 − 0.02) = 14.112/0.058333 = SEK 241.9200 million.

Step 3. Tax shields. TS1 = τc × rD × D0 = 0.206 × 0.05 × 104.1220 = 1.0725. The shield grows at 2% with the debt. The debt is rebalanced to 40% of value, so the shield is as risky as the line's assets and is discounted at rU:
PV(TS) = 1.0725/(0.078333 − 0.02) = SEK 18.3850 million

Step 4. NPV. VL = 241.9200 + 18.3850 = 260.3050, so NPV = 260.3050 − 234 = SEK 26.3050 million, the same as with the WACC method ✓.

What the check can catch. D0 came from the WACC value, so the match is a fixed point rather than an independent valuation. It still catches the two errors that happen: the wrong rate on the shield (at rD: 1.0725/(0.05 − 0.02) = 35.75 and NPV 43.67) and arithmetic slips.
criteria: Debt capacity D_0 = 0.40 × V^L_0 = 104.1220: 40% of the PV, not of the NPV (10.52).
PV(TS) = τ r_D D_0/(r_U − g) = 18.3850, discounted at r_U because D/V is constant. Discounting at r_D is the trap; a shield without growth understates PV(TS).
NPV = V^U + PV(TS) − 234 = 26.3050, equal to (d).

parts.label: f
parts.body: A colleague says the line's free cash flows should simply be discounted at rU, since rU reflects the risk of the line's assets. Is the colleague right? What does the gap between rwacc and rU capture?
parts.solution:
No. rU prices the risk of the line's assets but ignores the interest tax shield. Discounting the FCF at rU gives only VU = 241.92 and an NPV of 7.92, which leaves out the PV(TS) of 18.3850 that the 40% debt brings.

What the gap captures. rwacc = rU − d·τc·rD = 7.8333% − 0.4120% = 7.4213%. The 0.4120 percentage points are the tax shield written as a lower discount rate: the only difference between the two is the (1 − τc) on the cost of debt (recording 08, 1:24:02). APV makes the same correction by adding PV(TS) separately. The colleague would be right only for a line financed with equity alone, or without corporate tax.
criteria: No: r_U ignores the tax benefit of debt, so discounting at r_U gives V^U and understates the line's value and NPV.
The gap r_U − r_wacc = d·τ·r_D (0.412 percentage points) is the tax shield built into the discount rate; the only difference is (1 − τ) on r_D.
Bonus: r_U is right for an all-equity line or for discounting the tax shield in APV.

exercises.title: Real Options
exercises.merke: Som H2024 E6, men med usikker kontantstrøm · realopsjon 50 %
exercises.body:
Kuusijärvi Sahat Oy can build a new sawmill line for EUR 180 million, paid when it is built. The line then produces a cash flow every year forever, starting on the day it is built (built today: first cash flow at t = 0; built in one year: first cash flow at t = 1).

At today's lumber price the line would earn EUR 9 million at t = 0. At t = 1 the market settles in one of two states for good: from t = 1 on, the line earns EUR 13 million a year in the high state and EUR 6 million a year in the low state. Once the state is known, all cash flows are certain. The risk-free rate is 5% a year and does not change.

Nobody knows the probabilities of the states. Shares in Pohjan Puu Oyj, a listed sawmill company in the same market, trade at EUR 62.00 today, just after this year's dividend was paid. Pohjan Puu pays out all its cash flow: from t = 1 on, its dividend is EUR 4.00 per share a year forever in the high state and EUR 2.40 in the low state.

parts.label: a
parts.body: Suppose you wait and build the line at t = 1. What is the NPV of the line at t = 1 in each state?
parts.solution:
Built at t = 1, the line pays its first cash flow at once (at t = 1) and then every year forever. Its value at t = 1 is that cash flow plus a perpetuity from t = 2:

State at t = 1Value at t = 1NPV at t = 1
High13 + 13/0.05 = 273.00+93.00
Low6 + 6/0.05 = 126.00−54.00

The cash flow on the build date is the trap the lecture flags for a project that starts at once: many students «would forget about year zero» (recording 14, 19:47). Without it you get 80 and −60.
criteria: Includes the cash flow on the build date: value at t = 1 = C + C/0.05 = 21C.
Leaving out the t = 1 cash flow (80 and −60) is the trap.

parts.label: b
parts.body: What is the risk-neutral probability of the high state?
parts.solution:
Step 1. One traded claim, three values. Risk-neutral valuation needs a traded asset with a price today and a value at t = 1 in each state, all for the same claim. The Pohjan Puu share is that asset. Its price today, S0 = 62.00, is ex-dividend: it buys the dividends from t = 1 on. At t = 1 the holder receives that year's dividend and still owns a share worth the remaining dividends:

Su = 4.00 + 4.00/0.05 = 4.00 + 80.00 = 84.00
Sd = 2.40 + 2.40/0.05 = 2.40 + 48.00 = 50.40

Step 2. The formula sheet. ρ = [(1 + rf)S0 − Sd]/(Su − Sd) = (1.05 × 62.00 − 50.40)/(84.00 − 50.40) = (65.10 − 50.40)/33.60 = 14.70/33.60 = 0.4375, so 1 − ρ = 0.5625.

Check. ρ lies between 0 and 1. Also [0.4375 × 84.00 + 0.5625 × 50.40]/1.05 = (36.75 + 28.35)/1.05 = 65.10/1.05 = 62.00 returns today's price. This check cannot fail once ρ came from the same share, so it only catches slips. The real safeguard is step 1.

An equivalent route at t = 0. Value each dividend stream today: 62 = ρ × 4.00/0.05 + (1 − ρ) × 2.40/0.05 = 80ρ + 48(1 − ρ), so ρ = (62 − 48)/32 = 0.4375, the same answer, because C/0.05 today equals (C + C/0.05)/1.05.

The trap. Mixing the two routes, (1 + rf)S0 with the ex-dividend values 80 and 48, gives ρ = (65.10 − 48)/32 = 0.5344. That also lies between 0 and 1, so only the rule catches it: values at t = 1 include the payment made then, as with the lecture's traded annuity (recording 14, 1:10:26). The share does not have to be a copy of the line: any traded claim on the same two states gives the same ρ.
criteria: S_u and S_d are values at t = 1 including the dividend paid then: 84.00 and 50.40. S_0 = 62.00 is the price of the same claim (dividends from t = 1).

The t = 0 route 62 = 80ρ + 48(1 − ρ) gives the same 0.4375 and is equally accepted. 0.5344 comes only from combining (1 + r_f)S_0 with the ex-dividend values 80 and 48: wrong, although it lies between 0 and 1.
Uses (1 + r_f)S_0, the certainty equivalent, not S_0. Replication with Δ shares and a bond is equally accepted.
This part is the construction step: show the three values of the traded share and the formula.

parts.label: c
parts.body: What is the NPV of building the line today?
parts.solution:
Step 1. What building today gives. You pay 180 and receive 9 at once. From t = 1 the line pays 13 or 6 a year forever; at t = 1 that stream is worth 273 or 126, the values from (a) before the cost.

Step 2. Value the uncertain part with ρ. Any claim on the two states is worth its risk-neutral expectation discounted at rf:
[0.4375 × 273 + 0.5625 × 126]/1.05 = (119.4375 + 70.8750)/1.05 = 190.3125/1.05 = 181.2500

Step 3. NPV. NPV0 = −180 + 9 + 181.2500 = +10.2500 (EUR million). Building today has a positive NPV.

Shortcut: a perpetuity of C from t = 1 is worth C/0.05 today, so 0.4375 × 13/0.05 + 0.5625 × 6/0.05 = 113.75 + 67.50 = 181.25. Forgetting the 9 at t = 0 gives 1.25. Using 50/50 gives 19.00 and has no basis: the probabilities are unknown; ρ is what the market prices with.
criteria: Includes today's cash flow of 9 (the line starts at once).
Values the cash flows from t = 1 with ρ and discounts at r_f (no real probabilities are available).

parts.label: d
parts.body: What is the NPV today of waiting one year and deciding then? Do you build today or wait? Briefly comment.
parts.solution:
Step 1. The decision at t = 1. High state: build, +93. Low state: do not build, since the line would lose 54; the payoff is 0, not −54.

Step 2. Value today. NPVwait = [0.4375 × 93 + 0.5625 × 0]/1.05 = 40.6875/1.05 = 38.7500.

Decision: wait. 38.75 > 10.25, so waiting is worth 38.75 − 10.25 = 28.50 more than building today, even though building today has a positive NPV. Waiting costs today's 9 but saves the interest on paying 180 a year later (180 − 180/1.05 = 8.5714), a net cost of only 0.4286. In return you avoid building in the low state, which is worth 0.5625 × 54/1.05 = 28.9286 today: 28.9286 − 0.4286 = 28.50 ✓.
criteria: Compares the low state with 0 (you do not build), never with −54.
Decision: wait, because 38.75 > 10.25, although building today has a positive NPV.
Comment: waiting gives up today's cash flow (net of the interest saved) but avoids committing to the low state. Naming the lost cash flow and the avoided downside is enough.

parts.label: e
parts.body: Let X be the line's yearly cash flow in the low state, all else unchanged. For which X are you indifferent between building today and waiting?
parts.solution:
Step 1. Both NPVs as functions of X. A low-state stream of X from t = 1 is worth X + X/0.05 = 21X at t = 1. Building today:
−180 + 9 + [0.4375 × 273 + 0.5625 × 21X]/1.05 = −171 + 113.75 + 11.25X = −57.25 + 11.25X
Waiting: you still skip the low state as long as 21X < 180, so the value stays 38.75.

Step 2. Set them equal. −57.25 + 11.25X = 38.75 ⇒ X = 96.00/11.25 = 8.5333 (EUR million a year).

Check. 21 × 8.5333 = 179.20 < 180, so at this X the low state is still rejected when you wait, as step 1 assumed. Quick route: waiting costs 0.4286 (from (d)) and saves 0.5625 × (180 − 21X)/1.05. Setting them equal gives 180 − 21X = 0.80 and X = 8.5333.

Reading it. Building today beats waiting only if the low state is almost break-even (8.53 against the 8.57 that covers the cost). With a real downside, the option to wait is worth more than the small cost of waiting. The static break-even 8.5714 is not the answer: it ignores the net cost of waiting.
criteria: Writes the NPV of building today as a function of X (low-state value 21X at t = 1, weighted by 1 − ρ) and keeps the waiting value at 38.75.
Solves −57.25 + 11.25X = 38.75: X = 8.5333. The static break-even 180/21 = 8.5714 is not accepted.
Checks that 21X < 180, so the low state is still rejected when waiting.

parts.label: f
parts.body: What if the uncertainty about the future lumber price were very low, so that both states gave cash flows close to today's EUR 9 million? Would you build today or wait? Explain briefly.
parts.solution:
Build today. With very low volatility both states give cash flows close to 9, so at t = 1 the line is worth about 9 + 9/0.05 = 189 > 180 whatever happens. There is no bad state to avoid, so the option to wait is worth almost nothing, while waiting still costs today's cash flow net of the interest saved. The decision then follows today's NPV, which is positive.

The value of waiting comes from the downside you can walk away from: the higher the volatility, the more it is worth. It disappears as volatility goes to zero. The lecture makes the same point: with a very low σ the price stays close to today's level and the decision is the one you would take today, while a high σ makes waiting prudent (recording 14, 46:59 to 47:21).
criteria: Low σ: both states stay profitable, so there is no downside to avoid and the option to wait is worth (almost) nothing.
Decision: build today, since waiting loses today's cash flow and today's NPV is positive.
General point: the value of waiting rises with volatility. Linking to (e) is a bonus.

exercises.title: M&A
exercises.merke: Som H2025 E6, med tre måneder · M&A med regning 65 %
exercises.body:
Thyholm Industri A/S has announced a share offer for Mors Elektronik A/S: if the deal goes through, Mors shareholders receive 1 Thyholm share for every 2 Mors shares. The deal will either be completed or fail in exactly three months (T = 0.25 years). If it fails, both share prices return to their levels before the first rumours of the deal.

ThyholmMors
Share price before the rumours (DKK)280.00115.00
Share price today (DKK)268.00124.00
Shares outstanding (million)6050

The risk-free rate is 3% a year (annual compounding). Neither firm pays a dividend before T and short selling is allowed.

parts.label: a
parts.body: What is the offer worth per Mors share at today's prices? What premium does it offer over Mors's price before the rumours?
parts.solution:
One Mors share receives half a Thyholm share: 268.00/2 = DKK 134.00.

Premium over the price before the rumours: 134.00/115.00 − 1 = 16.5217%.

Mors trades at 124.00, DKK 10.00 below the offer: the market is not sure the deal goes through. That gap is what (b) and (c) turn into a probability.
criteria: Offer value at today's Thyholm price: 268/2 = 134.00.
Premium = 134/115 − 1 = 16.52% over the price before the rumours.
Using Thyholm's old price (280/2 = 140) is not the offer's value today.

parts.label: b
parts.body: Build a long-short position that buys 2 Mors shares today, is hedged with Thyholm shares and deposits the short-sale proceeds at the risk-free rate. What is your net outlay today? What is the position worth at T if the deal goes through? What is it worth if the deal fails?
parts.solution:
Step 1. The position. Two Mors shares become one Thyholm share if the deal goes through, so the hedge is to short one Thyholm share.

LegActionCash flow today
Long MorsBuy 2 shares at 124.00−248.00
Short ThyholmShort-sell 1 share at 268.00+268.00
DepositDeposit the 268.00 at the risk-free rate−268.00
Net outlay−248.00

The net outlay is DKK 248.00.

Step 2. Three months of interest. (1.03)0.25 = 1.007417, so the deposit grows to 268.00 × 1.007417 = 269.9878.

Step 3. Deal goes through. The 2 Mors shares are converted into the 1 Thyholm share you owe, so the share legs cancel and you keep the deposit: DKK 269.9878.

Step 4. Deal fails. Prices return to their levels before the rumours. You buy back 1 Thyholm share at 280 and sell the 2 Mors shares at 115: 269.9878 − 280 + 2 × 115 = DKK 219.9878.

Other constructions. The lecture also shows a self-financing version: short 1 Thyholm, buy 2 Mors and deposit only the rest, 268.00 − 248.00 = 20.00 (recording 16, 1:14:18). It costs 0 today and is worth 20.1483 or −29.8517 at T. It gives the same probability in (c).
criteria: Long 2 Mors and short 1 Thyholm (the exchange ratio), with the 268 deposited at r_f.
Net outlay = 248.00.
Interest for three months: 1.03^0.25 = 1.007417, so success = 269.9878. A whole year (1.03) is wrong.
Failure: 269.9878 − 280 + 230 = 219.9878, using the prices before the rumours.
This is the construction step of the exercise: show the legs, both payoffs and the interest factor.

parts.label: c
parts.body: What is the certainty equivalent of your outlay at T? What probability of completion does the market imply?
parts.solution:
Step 1. Certainty equivalent. The position cost 248.00 today. A fair price means its expected value at T must equal that outlay grown at the risk-free rate for three months: 248.00 × 1.007417 = DKK 249.8394. Setting the expected payoff equal to 248.00 is the error the H2025 key warns against.

Step 2. Solve for p.
249.8394 = p × 269.9878 + (1 − p) × 219.9878
249.8394 − 219.9878 = p × (269.9878 − 219.9878)
29.8517 = p × 50.00
p = 0.5970 (59.70%)

Check. 0.597033 × 269.9878 + 0.402967 × 219.9878 = 249.8394 ✓. The self-financing version gives the same: 0 = p × 20.1483 + (1 − p) × (−29.8517), so p = 0.5970.

The traps. Plugging in 248.00 instead of the certainty equivalent gives 56.02%; a whole year of interest gives 58.80%; no interest anywhere gives 60.00%.
criteria: Certainty equivalent = 248.00 × 1.03^0.25 = 249.8394, not 248.00 («very important to not just plug 100», H2025 key).
Solves CE = p × success + (1 − p) × failure: p = 59.70%.
Uses the three-month factor 1.03^0.25 throughout.
Any consistent construction (for example the self-financing one) is accepted if it gives the same p.

parts.label: d
parts.body: Use the change in each firm's market value since before the rumours to say whether the market expects the deal to create or destroy value. Who pays too much? Explain briefly.
parts.solution:
Thyholm: 60 × (268 − 280) = DKK −720 million. Mors: 50 × (124.00 − 115) = DKK +450 million. Together: −270 million.

Destroy. The combined value has fallen, so the market expects the deal to destroy value. Thyholm's shareholders pay too much: they lose more than Mors's shareholders gain, so the premium they pay exceeds anything the merger creates for them. Mors's shareholders capture the premium.

The changes are expectations: today's prices still include the chance that the deal fails (40%), so the effect if the deal goes through is larger.
criteria: Changes in market value: Thyholm −720, Mors +450, combined −270.
Conclusion: value is expected to be destroyed and Thyholm's shareholders overpay; Mors's shareholders gain.
An answer from the price changes alone (Thyholm down, Mors up) earns the conclusion points but not the number points.

parts.label: e
parts.body: Give one possible motive for the deal, other than synergies, that fits these price reactions. Explain in 2–3 sentences.
parts.solution:
Empire building. Thyholm's managers may want to run a larger company, since their pay, status and power grow with size. They are willing to pay a premium that Mors is not worth to Thyholm's shareholders. The market sees the overpayment, so Thyholm's price falls while Mors's shareholders, who receive the premium, gain.

Also accepted. Managerial hubris or overconfidence about running Mors better; diversification that Thyholm's shareholders could get more cheaply on their own; managers reducing the risk to their own jobs. Each must fit Thyholm down and Mors up. Tax savings from Mors's losses would be a value-creating motive and cannot explain a combined fall of 270 million (nor are they the answer the course expects); neither can «value creation» without a mechanism.
criteria: One motive other than synergies, explained in 2–3 sentences with its mechanism.
Consistent with the prices: the acquirer falls and the target rises, so the motive must make Thyholm's shareholders lose (empire building, hubris, diversification, managers' own interests).
Synergies or «value creation» alone earn nothing; a value-creating motive such as tax savings does not fit the combined fall in value.
